title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: During the intermission, a whiff of cold air came into Helene's box, the door opened, and Anatole entered, stooping and trying not to brush against anyone.
"Let me introduce my brother to you," said Helene, her eyes shifting uneasily from Natasha to Anatole.

Natasha turned her pretty little head toward the elegant young officer and smiled at him over her bare shoulder. Anatole, who was just as handsome up close as from a distance, sat down beside her and told her he had long wanted this pleasure — ever since the Naryshkins' ball, in fact, at which he had had the well-remembered pleasure of seeing her. Kuragin was much more natural and at ease with women than among men. He talked boldly and freely, and Natasha was strangely and pleasantly struck by the fact that there was nothing intimidating about this man who was so much talked about, but that on the contrary his smile was completely open, cheerful, and good-natured.
Kuragin asked her opinion of the performance and told her how at a previous performance Semenova had fallen down on the stage.

"And do you know, Countess," he said, suddenly addressing her as an old familiar acquaintance, "we're organizing a costume tournament; you ought to take part in it! It will be great fun. We're all meeting at the Kargins'! Please come! No, really, eh?" said he.

While saying this he never took his smiling eyes off her face, her neck, and her bare arms. Natasha knew for certain that he was captivated by her. This pleased her, yet his presence made her feel constrained and uneasy. When she wasn't looking at him she felt that he was looking at her shoulders, and she involuntarily caught his eye so that he would look into her eyes rather than at her body. But looking into his eyes she was frightened, realizing that the barrier of modesty she had always felt between herself and other men didn't exist between them. She didn't know how it was that within five minutes she had come to feel terrifyingly close to this man. They spoke of the most ordinary things, yet she felt that they were closer than she had ever been to any man. Natasha kept turning to Helene and to her father, as if asking what it all meant, but Helene was engaged in conversation with a general and didn't return her look, and her father's eyes said nothing but what they always said: "Having a good time? Well, I'm glad of it!"

During one of those moments of awkward silence when Anatole's prominent eyes were gazing calmly and steadily at her, Natasha, to break the silence, asked him how he liked Moscow. She asked the question and blushed. She felt the whole time that by talking to him she was doing something improper. Anatole smiled as though to encourage her.

"At first I didn't like it much, because what makes a city pleasant is the pretty women, isn't that so? But now I like it very much indeed," he said, looking at her meaningfully. "You'll come to the costume tournament, Countess? Do come!" and putting out his hand toward her bouquet and lowering his voice, he added, "You will be the prettiest there. Do come, dear countess, and give me this flower as a pledge!"
(The French phrase means: "Are the pretty women.")

Natasha didn't understand what he was saying any more than he did himself, but she felt that his incomprehensible words had an improper intention. She didn't know what to say and turned away as if she hadn't heard his remark. But as soon as she turned away she felt that he was there, behind her, so close behind her.

"How is he now? Confused? Angry? Should I set things right?" she asked herself, and she couldn't help turning around. She looked straight into his eyes, and his closeness, self-assurance, and the good-natured tenderness of his smile vanquished her. She smiled just as he was doing, gazing straight into his eyes. And again she felt with horror that no barrier existed between him and her.

The curtain rose again. Anatole left the box, calm and cheerful. Natasha went back to her father in the other box, now completely surrendered to the world she found herself in. Everything going on in front of her now seemed quite natural, but on the other hand all her previous thoughts of her fiance, of Princess Mary, or of life in the country didn't once enter her mind, as if they belonged to a remote past.

In the fourth act there was some kind of devil who sang while waving his arms about, till the boards were pulled out from under him and he disappeared below. That was the only part of the fourth act that Natasha saw. She felt agitated and tormented, and the cause of this was Kuragin, whom she couldn't help watching. As they were leaving the theater, Anatole came up to them, called their carriage, and helped them in. As he was handing Natasha in, he pressed her arm above the elbow. Agitated and flushed, she turned around. He was looking at her with glittering eyes, smiling tenderly.

Only after she had reached home was Natasha able to think clearly about what had happened to her, and suddenly remembering Prince Andrew she was horrified. At tea, to which everyone had sat down after the opera, she gave a loud cry, flushed, and ran out of the room.

"O God! I am lost!" she said to herself. "How could I let him?" She sat for a long time hiding her flushed face in her hands, trying to understand what had happened to her, but was unable either to grasp what had happened or what she felt. Everything seemed dark, confused, and terrible. There in that enormous, illuminated theater where the bare-legged Duport in a tinsel-decorated jacket jumped about to the music on wet boards, and young girls and old men, and the nearly naked Helene with her proud, calm smile, rapturously cried "bravo!" — there in the presence of that Helene it had all seemed clear and simple; but now, alone by herself, it was incomprehensible. "What is it? What was that terror I felt of him? What is this gnawing of conscience I'm feeling now?" she thought.

Only to the old countess at night in bed could Natasha have told all she was feeling. She knew that Sonya with her severe and simple views would either not understand it at all or be horrified at such a confession. So Natasha tried to work out what was tormenting her on her own.

"Am I ruined for Andrew's love or not?" she asked herself, and with comforting irony replied: "What a fool I am to ask that! What did happen to me? Nothing! I did nothing, I didn't lead him on at all. Nobody will know and I'll never see him again," she told herself. "So it's clear that nothing has happened and there's nothing to regret, and Andrew can love me still. But why 'still?' O God, why isn't he here?" Natasha calmed herself for a moment, but again some instinct told her that though all this was true, and though nothing had happened, yet the former purity of her love for Prince Andrew had been destroyed. And again in her imagination she went over her whole conversation with Kuragin, and again saw the face, gestures, and tender smile of that bold, handsome man when he pressed her arm.
